rpm_imperial.name: RPM Calculation (Imperial)

variables.D: Tool or workpiece diameter in inches

sources.title: Manufacturing Processes 4-5 - Unit 2: Speeds, Feeds, and Tapping
sources.author: LamNgeun Virasak
sources.excerpt: RPM = (CS × 4) / D where CS = Cutter speed in SFM, D = Tool diameter in inches. Note: 4 is approximation of 3.82
sources.notes: CC BY 4.0 Licensed textbook from Open Oregon Educational Resources

sources.title: Practical Machinist Forum - Why 3.82?
sources.excerpt: Number of inches in a foot - 12 divided by Pi - 3.14 = 3.8197 or 3.82. RPM = 3.82 × SFM ÷ tool diameter
sources.notes: Discussion explaining mathematical derivation: 12 inches/foot ÷ π

sources.title: Harvey Performance - Speeds and Feeds 101
sources.excerpt: The SFM calculation utilizes the industry standard of 3.82. The cutter diameter is multiplied by the speed or RPM, then divided by 3.82 to generate the SFM

validation_examples.description: 3/8 inch HSS end mill in mild steel (from Open Oregon example)

rpm_imperial.notes: Most fundamental machining formula. Constant 3.82 = 12/π. Some machinists use 4 for easier mental math. Derivation: circumference = πD, convert inches to feet (÷12), so RPM = SFM/(πD/12) = (SFM × 12)/(πD) = (SFM × 3.82)/D

rpm_metric.name: RPM Calculation (Metric)

variables.v: Cutting speed in meters per minute (m/min)
variables.D: Tool or workpiece diameter in millimeters

sources.title: Wikipedia - Speeds and Feeds
sources.excerpt: Cutting Speed (V) = [πDN]/1000 m/min where D=Diameter in millimeters, N=Spindle Speed in rpm. Can be rearranged to N = (V × 1000)/(π × D)
sources.notes: Wikipedia article with multiple citations. Formula can be rearranged for RPM calculation

sources.title: Keyence - Cutting Formulas
sources.excerpt: Metric formula for spindle speed: n = 1000 × v / (π × D)

rpm_metric.notes: Metric equivalent of imperial formula. Constant 318.3 = 1000/π. More precise value is 318.31. The 1000 factor converts meters to millimeters.

sfm_from_rpm.name: Surface Feet per Minute (SFM) from RPM

variables.D: Tool or workpiece diameter in inches

sources.title: Harvey Performance - Speeds and Feeds 101
sources.excerpt: The cutter diameter is multiplied by the speed or RPM, then divided by 3.82 to generate the SFM

sources.title: HSM Machining - General Speeds and Feeds Formulas
sources.excerpt: SFM = (Tool Diameter × RPM) / 3.82

sfm_from_rpm.notes: Inverse of RPM calculation formula. Used to determine actual cutting speed at a given spindle speed.

cutting_speed_metric.name: Cutting Speed (Metric) from RPM

variables.v: Cutting speed in meters per minute (m/min)
variables.D: Tool or workpiece diameter in millimeters
variables.1000: Conversion factor from mm to meters

sources.title: Wikipedia - Speeds and Feeds
sources.excerpt: Cutting Speed (V) = [πDN]/1000 m/min where D=Diameter in millimeters, N=Spindle Speed in rpm

sources.title: Machining Doctor - Cutting Speed Guide
sources.excerpt: V = πDN/1000 where V is cutting speed in m/min, D is diameter in mm, N is rpm

cutting_speed_metric.notes: Fundamental relationship: cutting speed = circumference × rotational speed. Circumference = πD (in mm), multiply by RPM to get mm/min, divide by 1000 to get m/min.

feed_rate_ipm.name: Feed Rate (Imperial) - IPM

variables.IPM: Feed rate in inches per minute
variables.N: Number of flutes (cutting edges) on the tool
variables.fz: Chip load (feed per tooth) in inches per tooth

sources.title: Manufacturing Processes 4-5 - Unit 2: Speeds, Feeds, and Tapping
sources.author: LamNgeun Virasak
sources.excerpt: IPM = F × N × RPM where F = Feed per tooth (inches), N = Number of teeth on cutter, RPM = Revolutions per minute
sources.notes: CC BY 4.0 Licensed. Example given: 0.002 × 2 × 960 = 3.84 IPM

sources.title: Harvey Performance - Speeds and Feeds 101
sources.excerpt: Feed Rate = RPM × Number of Flutes × Chip Load
sources.notes: Industry standard formula from major tool manufacturer

sources.title: CNC Cookbook - Chip Load Calculator
sources.excerpt: Feed Rate = RPM × number of flutes × chip load

validation_examples.description: Open Oregon example: 2-flute end mill at 960 RPM with 0.002 inch/tooth
4-flute end mill at 1000 RPM with 0.003 inch/tooth

feed_rate_ipm.notes: Feed rate is the linear speed at which the tool moves through the material. Must be balanced with spindle speed and chip load for optimal cutting.

chip_load.name: Chip Load (Feed per Tooth)

variables.fz: Chip load - feed per tooth (inches per tooth or mm per tooth)
variables.IPM: Feed rate (inches per minute or mm per minute)

sources.title: GDP Tooling - Chipload Calculator
sources.excerpt: Chip Load = Feed Rate (inches per minute) / (RPM × number of flutes)

sources.title: MellowPine - Chip Load Guide for Beginners
sources.excerpt: Chip Load (CL) = Feed Rate (FR) / (Spindle Speed (SS) × Number of Cutting Edges)

sources.title: Scarlett Inc - Chip Load Calculation
sources.excerpt: Chip load refers to the thickness of the material removed by each cutting edge during a single rotation. Formula: chip load = feed rate / (rpm × number of flutes)
sources.notes: Confirms formula and explains physical meaning

validation_examples.description: Reverse calculation of Open Oregon example

chip_load.notes: Chip load is independent of RPM and feed rate individually - it represents the actual thickness of material each tooth removes. Critical for tool life and surface finish. Too low = rubbing/heat, too high = tool breakage.

mrr_milling_metric.name: Material Removal Rate - Milling (Metric)

variables.MRR: Material Removal Rate in cubic centimeters per minute (cc/min or cm³/min)
variables.F: Feed rate in millimeters per minute (mm/min)
variables.1000: Conversion factor from mm³ to cm³

sources.title: Cadem - Material Removal Rate Formula
sources.excerpt: MRR = (D × W × F / 1000) cc/min where D is depth of cut (mm), W is width of cut (mm), and F is feed rate (mm/min)

sources.title: CNC Cookbook - Material Removal Rate: Optimizing MRR for Bigger Profits
sources.excerpt: MRR = Cut Width × Cut Depth × Feed Rate
sources.notes: Widely-used CNC reference confirming formula structure

sources.title: ZCS Mould - What Is Metal Removal Rate (MRR) in Machining?
sources.excerpt: MRR = depth of cut × width of cut × feed rate. Major variables are depth of cut, cut width, and feed rate

validation_examples.description: Shallow but wide cut with high feed rate

mrr_milling_metric.notes: MRR is the volume of material removed per unit time. Higher MRR = higher productivity but requires more machine power and rigidity. Limited by machine power, tool strength, and workholding.

mrr_milling_imperial.name: Material Removal Rate - Milling (Imperial)

variables.MRR: Material Removal Rate in cubic inches per minute (in³/min)
variables.F: Feed rate in inches per minute (IPM)

sources.title: CNC Cookbook - Material Removal Rate
sources.excerpt: MRR = Cut Width × Cut Depth × Feed Rate
sources.notes: Formula applies to both imperial and metric with appropriate units

sources.title: Montana State University - Milling Equations
sources.excerpt: Material removal rate calculations for milling operations
sources.notes: Academic source from university engineering department

validation_examples.description: Shallow wide cut: 0.1 inch depth × 1 inch width × 20 IPM

mrr_milling_imperial.notes: Imperial version of MRR formula. No unit conversion needed when all inputs are in inches. Useful for estimating machining time and power requirements.

mrr_turning_metric.name: Material Removal Rate - Turning (Metric)

variables.MRR: Material Removal Rate in cubic centimeters per minute (cc/min)
variables.F: Feed rate in millimeters per revolution (mm/rev)
variables.S: Cutting speed in meters per minute (m/min)

sources.title: Cadem - Material Removal Rate Formula
sources.excerpt: MRR = D × F × S cc/min where D is the depth of cut in mm, F is the feed rate in mm/rev and S is the cutting speed in m/min

sources.title: iLearn Engineering - Material Removal Rate Effects
sources.excerpt: For turning operations, MRR depends on depth of cut, feed per revolution, and cutting speed

mrr_turning_metric.notes: Turning MRR formula differs from milling because cutting is continuous rather than interrupted. Feed is per revolution rather than per minute.
